doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: The difficulty of making a living as a jazz writer; shrinking liner notes
summary: He describes vanishing outlets and the decline of liner notes as LPs gave way to CDs.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. Is it harder to make a living as a jazz writer than it is as a jazz musician?

Well I’ve never been a jazz musician. I think that’s a pretty hard road to go too. Being friends with musicians, not just in jazz but contemporary composed music or chamber music, this is not an easy way to make a living. I do not find it easy to make a living as a jazz writer, no I don’t. I’ve been doing it for 26, 27 years now, it hasn’t gotten any easier. I think that in the last couple of years especially there has been a great sad drain of outlets. For a while when the dot com world was new and burgeoning there was a lot of work that could be done on the web, good outlets. There were magazines that sprung up and now have disappeared, most recently Tower Pulse. Sound Aspects, that Dan Ouellette was editing for a couple of years had been a good outlet, now it’s gone. Music and Sound Output was another one that I was active with in the eighties. There’s been a retraction of publications. It has to do with our general economy in the U.S., it has to do with raising postage rates, it has to do with competition from the web and television and movies. I think with the hegemony of major companies that are pumping out a lot of hype around big pop stars and less interest in smaller niche audiences, there are a lot of cultural reasons for it. Right now there is a big retraction of liner notes, and I’ve always enjoyed writing liner notes because when you do a liner note you really are being exposed to the music, you’re one of the first people that gets exposed to it. And you kind of guide the listener who is going to buy this album into how to appreciate it, what went behind it. And if you write a good liner note I think it stays with the record for the life of the record. So I’ve liked doing that. But when they went from LPs to CDs, they turned the liner note from being a point of purchase stimulus.
When I would go through record stores I’d look at the liner note, read it standing there and decide whether I wanted to buy the thing or not.

Well now they’re on the inside of the jacket. You don’t see them until after you’ve bought the CD. So I was afraid for a long time that the record companies would catch on that this was no longer a valuable service that the writers were providing. But now they just don’t run liner notes because it’s another couple hundred dollars to the production budget and they can’t afford it.

Wow that’s unfortunate. And it’s so true, because I did the same thing. You obviously can’t hear the record when you’re holding it, but you can read about it. And that’s where I got a lot of my information, because there wasn’t all the publications out back then, and it’s a real art to writing good liner notes too.
